storm.summary_layperson: No storms on radar and the atmosphere is too weak to fuel much today, though there's a small, mostly-inland chance of an isolated shower or storm popping up this afternoon.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's moderate marine layer (74°F water vs 82°F air) would help choke anything that did try to cross it, but there's nothing on radar right now for it to act on.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows no storm cells anywhere near the cove as of 11:18 AM, and instability is weak — HRRR puts CAPE at just 170 J/kg, well below the threshold needed for organized convection. Bulk shear is modest too, around 10–14 kt through the window. The one active NWS product is an Air Quality Alert, which is unrelated to storm risk.

The Upton (OKX) forecast discussion does flag a small chance: a weak shortwave with a cold pool aloft "may spark an isolated shower/thunderstorm Saturday afternoon, especially north and west of NYC." That puts any activity well inland of Greenwich, not over the cove itself.

Local storm modifier: air is running about 8.1°F warmer than the Sound (82.4°F inland vs 74.3°F water), which builds a moderate stable marine layer over the water. protective_mechanism_active is technically false only because the delta hasn't crossed the 10°F trigger — but a moderate layer is still present and would work against any low-level convection that tried to cross onto the Sound.

Most likely outcome for the cove: dry with no thunder risk through the 11 AM–5 PM window. If anything does fire inland this afternoon, it's more likely to stay north/west of NYC than reach the immediate shoreline, and the marine layer gives the cove extra insurance even if a cell tried to drift this way.

What would change the call: any cell actually forming and showing up on KOKX radar within 50 mi, or CAPE building past the 500–1000 J/kg range the AFD mentions for after 6 PM (outside today's window, but worth watching into the evening).

wind.regime_label: Sea breeze reinforced by the background gradient

hourly.shift_note: sea breeze filling in, still ramping

wind.tactics_blurb: A sea-breeze day is filling in through midday — an 8°F air-water temperature gap is driving a SSW breeze that the light background wind is reinforcing rather than fighting, so expect it to build from light and patchy near 11 AM into a steady 9–10 kt by mid-afternoon. Pressure is fairly even across the cove with a slight edge toward the east side near the river mouth; start mid-line and don't overcommit to one side until the shifts settle into a rhythm after 2 PM.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a sea-breeze day reinforced by the background wind (internally: Regime A+). The air-water temperature gap driving the thermal is 8.1°F (82.4°F inland vs 74.3°F Sound water) — comfortably over the 5°F threshold needed to build a sea breeze. The background gradient wind is light and out of the south (~6 kt, authoritative station mean), which is an onshore direction — instead of opposing the thermal it adds to it, which is what makes this an A+ day rather than a pure thermal one.

Right now (11 AM) the sea breeze is still filling in: only about half of the stations closest to the cove (Old Greenwich / Riverside cluster) have flipped southerly, and RYC itself is reading a light 3.8 kt SSW with gusts to 6. That's consistent with an early-stage sea breeze rather than a fully mature one — expect it to firm up through midday as inland heating continues (temps were already 82°F at 11 AM with a forecast high of 85°F).

HRRR/obs divergence flag: the raw HRRR model forecast for this window is unreliable on direction — it has the wind swinging to E/SE at just 2–7 kt through the afternoon, a 118° divergence from what stations are showing right now (SSW, already established at RYC, KBDR, and KHPN alike). This is a case where the model is behind the obs; the hourly table above is built from the observed trend and the physics of a building A+ day, not the raw model output.

Where pressure sits: SSW flow is the cove's cleanest, most reliable direction — fairly even across the course, with maybe a touch more pressure near the mouth and the east shore (less shelter there than tucked against the west side).

Shift character: before about 2 PM, expect a persistent rightward creep in direction as the thermal ramps up rather than clean oscillations — don't fight it, just track it. After 2–3 PM, once the breeze matures, expect it to settle into normal 10–20° oscillations you can play tactically.

What racers will feel: light and patchy at the open (3–6 kt, drifter-ish), building into the sweet spot for one-design dinghies (9–10 kt) by mid-afternoon, with occasional gusts to 13–14 kt. No postponement risk from lack of breeze after the first hour or so.
